startScreenOptions.shortStartDescription: Interactive lecture with 5 embedded questions for IM17.1-IM17.9.

interactions.label: Which feature most reliably distinguishes cluster headache from migraine?

params.question: Which feature most reliably distinguishes cluster headache from migraine?

answers.text: Unilateral location of the pain

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Both migraine and cluster headache can be unilateral, so laterality alone does not distinguish them.

answers.text: Severe intensity of the pain

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Both migraine and cluster headache can produce severe pain; intensity alone is not a distinguishing criterion.

answers.text: Ipsilateral autonomic features such as tearing and nasal congestion

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Ipsilateral autonomic activation — tearing, nasal congestion, and partial Horner syndrome — is the defining hallmark of cluster headache and the trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias.

answers.text: Aggravation by routine physical activity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Worsening with routine activity is a diagnostic criterion for migraine, not cluster headache.

overallFeedback.feedback: Cluster headache is defined by ipsilateral autonomic features — tearing, nasal congestion, and partial Horner syndrome. These are absent in migraine, where nausea and photophobia dominate.
Ipsilateral autonomic activation (tearing, conjunctival injection, nasal congestion, partial Horner syndrome) is the hallmark that separates cluster headache from migraine.

params.question: A 52-year-old woman presents with the 'worst headache of her life' that reached maximum intensity within seconds. According to the SNNOOP10 framework, what is the primary significance of this mode of onset?

answers.text: It confirms a diagnosis of migraine with aura

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Migraine develops gradually and does not reach peak intensity within seconds. Thunderclap onset is a red flag for a secondary cause, not a feature of any primary headache.

answers.text: It is a red flag requiring urgent investigation to exclude subarachnoid haemorrhage

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Thunderclap onset (peak intensity within one minute) is a SNNOOP10 red flag. It demands immediate non-contrast CT followed by lumbar puncture if CT is normal, because re-bleed risk within 24 hours is 20–30%.

answers.text: It suggests a typical cluster headache attack

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Cluster headache produces severe periorbital pain with autonomic features, but its onset builds over minutes, not seconds. Thunderclap onset requires subarachnoid haemorrhage exclusion first.

answers.text: It indicates tension-type headache with acute exacerbation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Tension-type headache is bilateral, pressing, and builds gradually. A headache reaching peak intensity within seconds is a thunderclap — a SNNOOP10 red flag demanding urgent workup.

overallFeedback.feedback: Thunderclap onset — a headache reaching peak intensity within one minute — is a SNNOOP10 red flag pointing toward subarachnoid haemorrhage. It demands immediate CT and, if negative, lumbar puncture at ≥12 hours.
Thunderclap onset is one of the most critical SNNOOP10 red flags. The re-bleed risk of 20–30% within 24 hours and missed re-bleed mortality of 40–50% make urgent investigation mandatory.

params.question: A 45-year-old woman presents with headaches that are worst on waking and have been progressively worsening over 6 weeks. Examination reveals papilloedema and a sixth cranial nerve palsy. Which of the following best explains the sixth nerve palsy in this clinical context?

answers.text: Direct compression of the sixth nerve by a posterior fossa tumour

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While a posterior fossa lesion can directly compress the sixth nerve, an isolated sixth nerve palsy with papilloedema is more commonly a false-localising sign of raised intracranial pressure — it does not localise the lesion.

answers.text: A false-localising sign due to raised intracranial pressure

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The sixth cranial nerve has the longest intracranial course and is vulnerable to traction from diffusely raised pressure. Its palsy is a classic false-localising sign that does not indicate the lesion's location.

answers.text: Diabetic mononeuropathy affecting the sixth nerve

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Diabetic sixth nerve palsy typically presents in isolation without papilloedema. The combination of papilloedema with progressive morning headaches points to raised intracranial pressure.

answers.text: Demyelination affecting the abducens nucleus in the pons

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Pontine demyelination can cause sixth nerve palsy but would not produce papilloedema. The combination here points to raised ICP stretching the nerve along its long intracranial course.

overallFeedback.feedback: In this context, the sixth nerve palsy is a false-localising sign of raised intracranial pressure. The nerve's long intracranial course makes it susceptible to traction when pressure rises, regardless of the lesion's location.

A sixth nerve palsy with papilloedema and morning headaches is a classic raised ICP presentation. The sixth nerve's long intracranial course makes it uniquely vulnerable to traction from diffuse pressure elevation.

interactions.label: A lumbar puncture yields clear CSF with lymphocytic pleocytosis, raised protein,

params.question: A lumbar puncture yields clear CSF with lymphocytic pleocytosis, raised protein, a glucose ratio below 0.4, and an opening pressure of 28 cm H₂O. Which diagnosis does this CSF pattern most strongly suggest?

answers.text: Bacterial meningitis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Bacterial meningitis typically produces turbid, purulent CSF with a neutrophilic predominance. Although glucose is low in both, the lymphocytic picture and clear fluid argue against a bacterial cause.

answers.text: Viral meningitis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Viral meningitis is lymphocytic but characteristically shows normal CSF glucose. The low glucose ratio (<0.4) in this sample is the key finding that rules it out.

answers.text: Tuberculous meningitis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Lymphocytic pleocytosis with low glucose (ratio <0.4) and elevated protein is the hallmark CSF pattern of tuberculous meningitis. The raised opening pressure and clear fluid further support this diagnosis.

answers.text: Subarachnoid haemorrhage

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Subarachnoid haemorrhage produces uniformly blood-stained CSF across all four tubes, or xanthochromia in the supernatant — not a lymphocytic pleocytosis with low glucose.

overallFeedback.feedback: The critical pattern here is lymphocytic pleocytosis with low glucose. Viral meningitis has normal glucose (the key separator), bacterial meningitis is neutrophilic and turbid, and SAH produces bloody fluid — leaving tuberculous meningitis as the match.

Tuberculous meningitis characteristically shows lymphocytic pleocytosis, low glucose (CSF:serum ratio <0.4), and elevated protein. The key separator from viral meningitis is the glucose — viral meningitis preserves normal glucose.

params.question: A 30-year-old woman experiences migraine attacks on 6 days per month. She currently takes ibuprofen on 18 days per month for her headaches. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

answers.text: Start propranolol 40 mg daily for migraine prevention immediately

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Preventive therapy is indeed indicated (≥4 attacks/month), but starting it before addressing medication overuse will be ineffective. Preventive therapy should begin only after detoxification from the overused medication.

answers.text: Switch from ibuprofen to sumatriptan for all attacks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Switching the abortive agent does not address the underlying medication-overuse headache. Triptans carry the same overuse risk at ≥10 days per month and would perpetuate the cycle.

answers.text: Detoxify from medication-overuse headache first, then start preventive therapy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. She meets criteria for medication-overuse headache (analgesics ≥15 days/month). Preventive therapy should only begin after detoxification — painkillers taken this frequently paradoxically worsen headaches.

answers.text: Increase ibuprofen dose to 800 mg to reduce attack frequency

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Escalating the analgesic dose worsens the medication-overuse cycle. The solution is reducing medication use — fewer analgesic days, not higher doses.

overallFeedback.feedback: This patient has medication-overuse headache (analgesics ≥15 days/month). Preventive therapy (propranolol or topiramate) is indicated, but it must begin only after detoxification from the overused medication — otherwise it will not work.

Medication-overuse headache must be addressed before starting preventive therapy. Analgesics taken on ≥15 days per month paradoxically increase headache frequency — the way out is reducing medication use, not escalating it.
